summary: This standard describes how IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies are encapsulated for transmission over FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network technology. It lets IP hosts and routers share an FDDI network.

plainLanguage.summary: FDDI is an old fibre-optic ring network with its own frame format and its own kind of hardware address. This RFC says exactly how to wrap an IP datagram or an ARP message so that it can travel across an FDDI network, and which numbers to use at each layer so that different implementations agree. It also fixes the largest packet that may be sent, at 4352 octets.

subtitle: How IP datagrams and ARP messages are wrapped in LLC/SNAP so they can cross a fibre-optic FDDI ring.

tldr.problem: FDDI is a fibre-optic local network with its own frame format and its own kind of hardware address, so IP hosts and routers need an agreed way to put datagrams and ARP messages on it that works the same on every implementation.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP packets ride inside IEEE 802.2 LLC Type 1 frames with a SNAP header carrying the EtherType. ARP maps 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses, and the MTU is fixed at 4352 octets.
tldr.outcome: Stations on FDDI can interoperate with each other and, through translational bridges, with Ethernet stations. This RFC is an Internet Standard (STD 36) and no newer RFC is recorded as replacing it.

today: RFC 1390 is an Internet Standard, STD 36, published in January 1993. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself says nothing about current use of FDDI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The goal of the specification is to allow compatible and interoperable implementations for transmitting IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies.

The Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) specifications define a family of standards for Local Area Networks that provides the Physical Layer and Media Access Control Sublayer of the Data Link Layer as defined by the ISO Open System Interconnection Reference Model. The family of FDDI standards corresponds to the IEEE 802 MAC layer standards. The remainder of the Data Link Service is provided by the IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control service, so the stack of services has IP and ARP at the top, then 802.2 LLC, then the FDDI MAC, PHY and PMD layers.

At this time it is not necessary that the use of IP and ARP be consistent between FDDI and IEEE 802 networks, but the intent of the memo is not to preclude Data Link Layer interoperability at such time as the standards define it. It is the explicit intent of the memo to allow the interoperability of IP and ARP between stations on FDDI networks and stations on Ethernet networks via translational bridges.

The FDDI standards define both single and dual MAC stations. This document describes the use of IP and ARP on single MAC stations, whether single-attach or dual-attach, only.
sections.plainLanguage: FDDI provides the bottom two layers of the network stack. Logical Link Control, or LLC, sits on top of it and offers the rest of the link service. This memo describes how IP and ARP use that service, and it is written so that an FDDI station and an Ethernet station can still talk to each other through a bridge.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies sent on FDDI networks shall be encapsulated within the 802.2 LLC and Sub-Network Access Protocol data link layers and the FDDI MAC and physical layers. The SNAP must be used with an Organization Code indicating that the SNAP header contains the EtherType code.

802.2 LLC Type 1 communication, which must be implemented by all conforming 802.2 stations, is used exclusively. All frames must be transmitted in standard 802.2 LLC Type 1 Unnumbered Information format, with the DSAP and the SSAP fields of the 802.2 header set to the assigned global SAP value for SNAP. The 24-bit Organization Code in the SNAP must be zero, and the remaining 16 bits are the EtherType from Assigned Numbers: IP is 2048 and ARP is 2054.

The total length of the LLC header and the SNAP header is 8 octets. The DSAP and SSAP value K1 is 170 decimal, the Organization Code value K2 is 0, and the control value is 3, which is Unnumbered Information.
sections.plainLanguage: Every FDDI frame carrying IP or ARP has an eight-octet header above the FDDI MAC header. The first three octets are the 802.2 LLC part and the last five are the SNAP part. Two of the octets carry the fixed value 170, one carries the value 3, three must be zero, and the last two carry 2048 for IP or 2054 for ARP.

sections.title: Address Resolution, Broadcast and Multicast
sections.content:
The mapping of 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses shall be done via the dynamic discovery procedure of the Address Resolution Protocol. Internet addresses are assigned arbitrarily on Internet networks, so each host's implementation must know its own Internet address and respond to Address Resolution requests appropriately, and it must also use ARP to translate Internet addresses to FDDI addresses when needed.

ARP has several fields that parameterize its use in any specific context: a 16-bit Hardware Type Code, a 16-bit Protocol Type Code, an 8-bit octet count for each hardware address, an 8-bit octet count for each protocol address, and a 16-bit Operation Code. The hardware type code assigned for IEEE 802 networks is 6 and the one assigned for Ethernet networks is 1. Differing values between Ethernet and IEEE 802 networks cause interoperability problems in bridged environments, so in order not to preclude interoperability with Ethernets in a bridged environment, ARP packets shall be transmitted with a hardware type code of 1, and shall be accepted if received with a hardware type code of 1. The protocol type code for IP is 2048, the hardware address length is 6, the protocol address length for IP is 4, and the operation code is 1 for request and 2 for reply.

To avoid precluding interoperability in a bridged environment, the hardware addresses in ARP packets, ar$sha and ar$tha, must be carried in canonical bit order, with the Group bit positioned as the low order bit of the first octet. As FDDI addresses are normally expressed with the Group bit in the high order bit position, the addresses must be bit-reversed within each octet.

The broadcast Internet address, the address on that network with a host part of all binary ones, must be mapped to the broadcast FDDI address, of all binary ones.

A method of supporting IP multicasting is specified in the host extensions document, and that method shall be used in FDDI networks if IP multicasting is to be supported. An IP multicast address is mapped to an FDDI group address by placing the low order 23 bits of the IP address into the low order 23 bits of the FDDI group address 01-00-5E-00-00-00 in canonical order. The IP multicast address 224.255.0.2 therefore maps to the FDDI group address 01-00-5E-7F-00-02, and when bit-reversed for transmission in the destination MAC address field of an FDDI frame it becomes 80-00-7A-FE-00-40, with the multicast or group bit as the high order bit of the first octet, that being the first bit transmitted on the medium.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP is how a host turns an IP address into the hardware address of its neighbour. On FDDI the hardware address is 48 bits, and the memo insists on using the same ARP hardware type code as Ethernet, 1, so that a bridge can connect the two. FDDI also writes hardware addresses in the opposite bit order from Ethernet, so the memo spells out the reversal.

sections.title: Packet Size and MAC Layer Rules
sections.content:
The FDDI MAC specification defines a maximum frame size of 9000 symbols, 4500 octets, for all frame fields including four symbols, two octets, of preamble. This leaves roughly 4470 octets for data after the LLC/SNAP header is taken into account. In order to allow future extensions to the MAC header and frame status fields, it is desirable to reserve additional space for MAC overhead. Therefore, the MTU of FDDI networks shall be 4352 octets. This provides for 4096 octets of data and 256 octets of headers at the network layer and above. Implementations must not send packets larger than the MTU.

Gateway implementations must be prepared to accept packets as large as the MTU and fragment them when necessary, and should be able to accept packets as large as can be carried within a maximum size FDDI frame and fragment them. Host implementations should be prepared to accept packets as large as the MTU, but hosts must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they have explicit knowledge that the destination is prepared to accept them. A host may communicate its size preference in TCP-based applications via the TCP Maximum Segment Size option. There is no minimum packet size restriction on FDDI networks.

Some versions of Unix 4.x bsd use a different encapsulation method in order to get better network performance with the VAX virtual memory architecture. Hosts directly connected to FDDI networks shall not use trailers. The IP datagram is transmitted over FDDI networks as a series of 8-bit bytes, a byte transmission order that has been called big-endian.

The FDDI MAC specification does not require that 16-bit and 48-bit address stations be able to interwork fully, but it does require that 16-bit stations have full 48-bit functionality. To avoid interoperability problems, only 48-bit addresses shall be used with IP and ARP. Only the use of Unrestricted tokens and Asynchronous frames are required for FDDI interoperability, so all IP and ARP frames shall be transmitted as Asynchronous LLC frames using Unrestricted tokens, and the priority value is a matter of local convention. To avoid precluding interoperability with Ethernet in a bridged environment, FDDI implementations must be prepared to receive and ignore trailing pad octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The MTU on FDDI is fixed at 4352 octets, with room kept aside for headers. Hosts must not send more than 576 octets unless they know the other end can take it, and gateways have to fragment anything larger than the MTU. All IP and ARP frames go out as asynchronous frames using unrestricted tokens.

sections.title: IEEE 802.2 Details
sections.content:
While not necessary for supporting IP and ARP, all implementations must support IEEE 802.2 standard Class I service in order to be compliant with 802.2. Class I LLC requires the support of Unnumbered Information commands, eXchange IDentification commands and responses, and TEST link commands and responses. Stations need not be able to transmit XID and TEST commands, but must be able to transmit responses.

Command frames are identified by having the low order bit of the SSAP address reset to zero, and response frames have that bit set to one. The UI command has an LLC control field value of 3. The XID command or response has a control field value of 175 if the Poll/Final bit is off, or 191 if it is on. The TEST command or response has a control field value of 227 if the Poll/Final bit is off, or 243 if it is on.

UI responses and UI commands with the Poll bit set shall be ignored, and UI commands having other than the SNAP SAP in the DSAP or SSAP fields shall not be processed as IP or ARP packets. When an XID or TEST command is received, an appropriate response must be returned, and only if the DSAP is the SNAP SAP, 170 decimal, the Null SAP, 0 decimal, or the Global SAP, 255 decimal. The Final bit in the response must be copied from the Poll bit in the command. XID response frames must include an 802.2 XID Information field of 129.1.0 indicating Class I, connectionless, service, and TEST response frames must echo the information field received in the corresponding TEST command frame.
sections.plainLanguage: Beyond sending and receiving IP, an FDDI station still has to behave like a proper 802.2 station. It has to answer the LLC housekeeping commands XID and TEST, with fixed control values, and it has to ignore anything that is not addressed to the SNAP service address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document records only that fact: it describes the encapsulation and the MAC layer rules for carrying IP and ARP over FDDI, and says nothing about who may send what or how the traffic is protected.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not discuss security. It only says so in as many words.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1188
sections.content: The memo summarises the differences between RFC 1188 and itself. A reference to a future dual-MAC document has been removed. A statement of explicit intent to support FDDI and Ethernet interoperability has been added. The acceptance of ARP frames bearing hardware type code 6, IEEE 802, has been removed. The references have been updated, and the author's address has been updated.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with RFC 1188, this version adds a clear statement that FDDI and Ethernet are meant to interoperate, drops the reference to a dual-MAC document that was never written, and no longer accepts ARP frames that carry the IEEE 802 hardware type code.

fields.desc: The EtherType from Assigned Numbers. IP is 2048, ARP is 2054.
